problems.field: eligibility.criterion_1 (conclusion under check: people were randomly assigned to generative-AI assistance)
problems.form_value: The conclusion under check reads the six arms as random assignment to generative-AI assistance. The form itself codes criterion_1 'unclear' and leaves the call to Review 1.
problems.source_says: The AI-versus-human factor randomizes a belief about the source of the same material, not AI assistance. The paper calls the source 'perceived' (H1) and the lists 'purportedly' from a human or ChatGPT (Abstract). It separates 'the actual information provided' from 'the perception of the collaborator' (p. 3). No participant used an AI tool, and every arm saw an example. The source contrasts therefore fail criterion 1. Only the level contrasts remain (problems 3 and 4).
problems.quote: Why did low-creativity ChatGPT assistance hinder participant creativity when the same assistance from a human did not?
problems.locator: p. 7, Discussion, right column, first paragraph; p. 1, Abstract; p. 3, Section 2.1 (last sentence) and Hypothesis 1; p. 4, Section 3.2 and Figure 1

problems.form_value: ChLo, ChTy, ChHi = generative_ai; HuLo, HuTy, HuHi = other_aid
problems.source_says: At each level both labels got the same list: Table 2 prints three lists for six arms. Paired arms therefore cannot differ in whether the material is AI output, and the codes record only what participants were told. If the low list is ChatGPT output, as the Discussion says (p. 7), HuLo also received ChatGPT text and other_aid is wrong. If it is not, ChLo received no AI output and generative_ai is wrong.
problems.quote: Thus, participants in the “low” creativity condition (regardless of source) received a unique list of nouns (Table 2); participants in the “typical” creativity condition (regardless of source) received a different and unique list of nouns;
problems.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3 Priming, second paragraph, and Table 2

problems.field: ai_tool.role (and check c: is the material generative-AI output)
problems.form_value: ideas_supplied (codebook: 'the study hands participants AI-generated ideas or examples')
problems.source_says: The Methods never say who produced the lists. They say the creativity level was 'determined from' 102 ChatGPT responses and that each list 'was selected' at a percentile rank (PR). The low list's PR (0.05 in the text, 0.03 in Table 2) is below the 31.03 to 99.60 range the paper reports for GPT-4 results in Cropley (2023) (p. 2). The paper does not say whether the 102 responses are those results. Its 'ChatGPT Output' and 'generated by ChatGPT' (Figure 2 axis, p. 7) follow the label, because Figure 2 calls the same lists 'Human Output' in the student-labeled arms. No model or version is named, and no participant used a tool.
problems.quote: The creativity level of the list of nouns was determined from a sample (Cropley 2023) of ChatGPT responses (N = 102) with a mean Percentile Rank (relative to human norms) of 64.93 (SD = 21.75).
problems.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3 Priming (end of left column into right column) and Table 2 header; p. 2, left column, first paragraph; p. 6, Figure 2 x-axis labels; p. 7, Discussion, second paragraph

problems.field: contrasts (ChLo vs ChTy, ChHi vs ChTy).comparison_type; arms[ChTy].description
problems.form_value: ai_design, with ChTy as control because the typical list 'is the default configuration'
problems.source_says: The paper never calls the typical list a default or the creativity levels AI configurations. It says only that the typical list was chosen to sit near the ChatGPT mean. Level is a property of the example, crossed with the label: the student-labeled arms got the same three lists. The AI element in these two contrasts is the shared 'ChatGPT' label on lists of unstated origin (problem 3). 'Another AI configuration' is the form's inference, not the paper's statement.
problems.quote: Note that the typical creativity list was selected to be as close to the mean of ChatGPT responses as possible.
problems.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3 Priming (right column, first paragraph) and Table 2; p. 4, Section 3.2

problems.field: ai_available_when_produced (bears on check b: was AI material available for the participant's own work)
problems.source_says: The paper does not say the list stayed on screen during the DAT. Figure 1 shows prime, rating, and DAT as successive steps, and the DAT rules ask participants to think of the words on their own. The text supports a one-time example shown and rated before the task, not AI help available while participants wrote the scored list. The form marks this field 'Kept as yes, not confirmed.'
problems.quote: Think of the words on your own (e.g., do not just look at objects in your surroundings).
problems.locator: p. 5, Section 3.5.2.2, DAT rule 5; p. 4, Section 3.2 and Figure 1

confirmed.statement: The paper states random allocation in four places: 'before being randomly allocated to one of six priming conditions' and 'The random allocation to priming conditions resulted in the following groups (Table 1)' (Section 3.1), 'Participants were then randomly allocated to one of six priming conditions' (Section 3.2), and 'After random allocation to the priming condition' (Section 3.3). The form's assignment quote is verbatim.
confirmed.locator: p. 3, Section 3.1, first and second paragraphs; p. 4, Section 3.2; p. 4, Section 3.3, second paragraph

confirmed.statement: Unit = individual and structure = between are right. Each participant was allocated to one cell of a 2 x 3 factorial, rated 'the prime they received', and the DAT was analyzed with a one-way between-groups ANOVA. No condition order needs checking (check e does not apply).
confirmed.locator: p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 4, Figure 1; p. 5, Section 4.1

confirmed.statement: assignment.what_was_assigned matches the source: one seven-noun example DAT response, said to come from 'a student' or 'ChatGPT', with its creativity level withheld. Participants retyped it, rated it, and then completed the DAT themselves.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2; p. 4, Section 3.3, second paragraph

confirmed.statement: Allocation counts match arms[].n_randomized: Human 56, 69, 67; ChatGPT 53, 74, 68; total 387. Per-arm analyzed counts are not printed, so n_analyzed = null is right.
The three lists in the arm descriptions match Table 2 word for word, including the spelling 'Elixer'.
Coding the three source contrasts (ChLo vs HuLo, ChTy vs HuTy, ChHi vs HuHi) as 'other' fits the text: each pair saw the identical list under a different stated source.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3, second paragraph; p. 7, Discussion, right column

confirmed.statement: ai_tool.name_model is right: the Methods name only 'ChatGPT', with no model or version. GPT-4 appears only in the introduction's account of Cropley (2023).
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3; p. 2, left column, first paragraph

confirmed.statement: ai_tool.how_used is accurate: no participant used an AI tool. The procedure runs demographics, covariates, prime (retyped), rating, DAT, attention check.

The only textual basis for reading the ChatGPT-labeled arms as AI assistance is the paper's framing: it studies 'the possible impact of an AI assistant (ChatGPT), compared to a human assistant', and H1 calls the prime 'assistance given'.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3, first paragraph; p. 3, Hypothesis 1

confirmed.statement: preregistered = not_stated is right: the paper mentions no preregistration, registry, or OSF page.

summary: The PDF confirms that individual students were randomly allocated, between subjects, to six priming conditions (pp. 3-4), but the AI factor is a label on identical seven-noun lists said to come from 'a student' or 'ChatGPT', no participant used an AI tool, and the paper itself calls the source 'perceived' and 'purportedly' ChatGPT, so the source contrasts do not vary generative-AI assistance. The arm codes generative_ai and other_aid, the role ideas_supplied, and the ai_design level contrasts rest on lists whose ChatGPT origin the Methods never state (the low list's percentile rank is below the GPT-4 range the paper reports), so criterion 1 fails for the source contrasts and is unclear for the level contrasts.
